entry: Process by which the information in a [[Gene|gene]] is used to produce a functional product, such as a [[Protein|protein]] or a functional [[RNA]] molecule. [[Transcription (biology)|Transcription]] copies the gene's sequence into RNA, which in [[Eukaryote|eukaryotes]] is performed in the nucleus by three types of RNA polymerase. Protein-coding genes yield messenger RNA that is [[Translation (biology)|translated]] into amino acid chains that fold into proteins, while non-coding genes produce RNA that itself performs a cellular role. Expression is regulated by transcription factors and epigenetic modifications such as DNA methylation, and it responds to cellular needs and environmental change, although some genes are expressed continuously. Dysregulated expression underlies diseases including [[Cancer|cancers]] and genetic disorders such as cystic fibrosis.

Study of [[Family|families]], family history and the tracing of [[Lineage (anthropology)|lineages]]. Genealogists use oral interviews, historical records, genetic analysis and other sources to demonstrate [[Kinship|kinship]] and pedigrees, presenting results as charts or narratives. In the narrow sense, a genealogy or family tree traces the descendants of one person, while a family history traces that person's ancestors, although the terms are often used interchangeably. Family history is broader, adding biography, traditions and community history. Amateurs usually research their own ancestry, while professionals may research for others, publish methods books or produce databases. Motives include curiosity about heritage, especially where records were lost through [[Adoption|adoption]] or [[Divorce|divorce]], scholarly or forensic work, and tracing legal next of kin under intestacy laws. Autosomal [[DNA]] analysis now confirms documentary links and identifies unknown relatives through shared genomic segments.

American single-engine, supersonic multirole [[Fighter aircraft|fighter]] developed by General Dynamics and produced by [[Lockheed Martin]] since 1993. Designed as an air superiority day fighter, it evolved into an all-weather multirole aircraft, with over 4,600 built since 1976. Its features include a [[Turbofan|turbofan]] engine and fly-by-wire flight controls. From 1978 it replaced the F-105, A-7 and F-4 in U.S. Air Force tactical roles and has flown combat in the [[Gulf War]], Bosnia, Afghanistan, Libya and [[Iraq]] and Syria. Approximately 2,102 aircraft of the F-16 family were operational as of 2026, about 15% of active combat aircraft, and many countries are replacing it with the [[Lockheed Martin F-35 Lightning II|F-35 Lightning II]].

Former American multinational [[Conglomerate (company)|conglomerate]] (1892–2024). Formed in 1892 by merging [[Thomas Edison]]'s Edison General Electric Company with the Thomson-Houston Electric Company, a consolidation orchestrated by financier [[J. P. Morgan]], it played a role in electric power, electric light, home appliances, aviation and medical imaging. Its divisions covered aerospace, energy, healthcare, lighting, locomotives, appliances and finance. Two employees, Irving Langmuir and Ivar Giaever, won the [[Nobel Prize]]. From 1986 until 2013 it owned the [[NBC]] television network. After the [[Great Recession]] it sold divisions, and in November 2021 its final CEO, Larry Culp, announced a breakup into three public companies. GE Aerospace kept the General Electric name and ticker, GE HealthCare was spun off in 2023, and GE Vernova became the energy company.

American daytime television [[Soap opera|soap opera]] created by Frank and Doris Hursley, broadcast on ABC since April 1, 1963. Set in the fictional city of Port Charles, New York, it is taped in Los Angeles. From 1979 to 1988 it drew more viewers than any other daytime soap, helped by the "supercouple" Luke and Laura, whose 1981 wedding drew 30 million viewers, the highest-rated hour in American soap opera history. Guinness World Records lists it as the longest-running American soap opera in production. It holds the record for most Daytime Emmy Awards for Outstanding Drama Series, with 14 wins.

American multinational automotive company headquartered in [[Detroit]], Michigan. GM owns four core brands, [[Chevrolet]], Buick, GMC and Cadillac, and operates manufacturing plants in eight countries. It was the largest automaker in the United States by total sales and was the largest in the world for 77 years before losing the title to [[Toyota]] in 2008. Durant formed the General Motors Company in 1908 as a holding company for Buick, borrowing its naming convention from [[General Electric]]. Early acquisitions included Olds, Cadillac and Oakland, later Pontiac. Durant co-founded Chevrolet in November 1911, and Chevrolet was consolidated into GM in 1918. The current entity was established in 2009 after a Chapter 11 reorganization. As of 2024 GM ranked 25th on the Fortune 500 by total revenue. In 2021 it announced an intent to end production of [[Internal combustion engine|internal combustion engine]] vehicles by 2035, plans mostly scaled back in 2025.

Geometric theory of gravitation published by [[Albert Einstein]] in May 1916. It generalizes [[Special relativity|special relativity]] and refines the law of universal gravitation of [[Isaac Newton]]. It describes gravity as a geometric property of four-dimensional [[Spacetime|spacetime]], in which the curvature of spacetime is related to the energy, momentum and stress of matter and radiation through the [[Einstein field equations]]. Newton's law is a prediction of the theory for the almost flat spacetime around stationary masses. Predictions beyond Newtonian physics include gravitational time dilation, gravitational lensing, the gravitational redshift of light and [[Black hole|black holes]]. Gravitational waves have been observed directly by the LIGO collaboration. The theory underpins modern cosmology, including the [[Big Bang]] and cosmic microwave background radiation. No self-consistent [[Quantum gravity|quantum gravity]] theory has been found, and gravity has not yet been unified with the strong, weak and electromagnetic interactions.

Branch of mathematics, also called point-set topology, that deals with the basic set-theoretic definitions and constructions used in [[Topology|topology]]. Its fundamental concepts are continuity, compactness and connectedness, defined by means of [[Open set|open sets]]. A topology on a set X is a family of subsets containing the empty set and X, closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections, and a set with a topology is a [[Topological space|topological space]]. Different choices of open sets yield different notions of continuity. [[Metric space|Metric spaces]], in which a distance is defined between points, form an important class of topological spaces. A basis generates a topology, and subspace, product and quotient topologies extend the construction. General topology emerged from the study of subsets of the real line, the manifold concept and normed spaces, and took its present form around 1940. It is the foundation for [[Algebraic topology|algebraic topology]], differential topology and geometric topology.

Demographic cohort succeeding [[Generation Z]], born from the early 2010s to the mid-2020s. Named after the first letter of the [[Greek alphabet]], it is the first generation born entirely in the 21st century. The name originated in a 2008 survey by Australian consultancy McCrindle Research. Most members are children of younger Generation X, [[Millennials]] and older Generation Z. They are the first full generation not to have known a world without [[Smartphone|smartphones]] and [[Social media|social media]]. They experienced the [[COVID-19 pandemic]] as young children. Studies link screen time with health problems including [[Myopia|myopia]] and [[Obesity|obesity]].

Demographic cohort following the [[Baby boomers|baby boomers]] and preceding [[Millennials]], usually defined as people born from 1965 to 1980. As children in the 1970s and 1980s they were called the "Latchkey Generation" for returning to empty homes, a result of rising [[Divorce|divorce]] rates and increased maternal workforce participation. As young adults they were dubbed the "[[MTV]] Generation" and characterized as slackers. In their youth they experienced the last days of [[Communism|communism]] in the [[Soviet Union]] and the [[Eastern Bloc]]. In midlife, research describes Gen Xers as active, happy and entrepreneurial, with a work–life balance.

Demographic cohort succeeding [[Millennials]], typically defined as people born from 1997 to 2012. Also called Gen Z or Zoomers, its members grew up with the internet, watching online videos, often on [[YouTube]], and playing online games. As adolescents and young adults they were dubbed "digital natives". The generation has been described as "better behaved and less hedonistic" than previous ones, with fewer teenage pregnancies and less alcohol consumption. It reports greater awareness and diagnosis of [[Mental health|mental health]] conditions and more sleep deprivation, and screen-time harms were most pronounced in adolescents. Members have been active in politics, using [[Social media|social media]] for mobilization.

All individuals born and living at about the same time, regarded collectively. In kinship, the term designates the parent–child relationship. In demographics and social science it is a synonym for birth cohort, people who experience the same significant events within a given period. The average familial generation is about 20–30 years. In developed nations it is in the high 20s, having risen since the late 18th century with [[Industrialisation|industrialization]], urbanization and later first pregnancies, while in less-developed nations it remains in the low 20s. Social generations became a concept in the 19th century, when modernization and youth-centered political rhetoric encouraged dividing society by age. Critics argue that generational differences often reflect age and period effects rather than enduring traits.

Subfield of [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]] that uses generative models to create text, images, video, audio, code or other digital data in response to input, usually natural-language prompts. Its prevalence grew after the [[AI boom]] of the early 2020s, made possible by [[Large language model|large language models]] built on the transformer architecture. Applications include the chatbots [[ChatGPT]] and Claude, Google Gemini, and image generators such as DALL-E and Midjourney. Models can produce incorrect answers, or "hallucinations", and have been used for cybercrime and deepfakes. They have been trained on [[Copyright|copyrighted]] works without rightholders' permission, and their [[Data center|data centers]] consume fresh water and growing amounts of energy.

English rock band formed in 1967 at Charterhouse School in [[Surrey]]. Among the pioneers of progressive rock in the 1970s, with [[Peter Gabriel]] as frontman, Genesis moved to a pop-oriented sound in the 1980s, with *Invisible Touch* (1986) and *We Can't Dance* (1991) achieving massive commercial success. With 100 million to 150 million albums sold, it ranks among the best-selling artists. It won a Grammy Award for Best Concept Music Video for "Land of Confusion" and was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2010. After *Calling All Stations* (1997) the band disbanded until reunion tours in 2007 and 2021.

Set of rules by which living cells translate information in [[DNA]] or [[RNA]] sequences into [[Protein|proteins]]. Codons, triplets of nucleotides, specify [[Amino acid|amino acids]]; the code can be expressed as a table of 64 entries, and with some exceptions each codon specifies a single amino acid. The [[Ribosome|ribosome]] links amino acids in the order specified by messenger RNA, using transfer RNA to carry them. The code is nearly universal, with variant codes in [[Mitochondria|mitochondria]]. In 1955 [[Francis Crick]] proposed in an unpublished note that an adaptor molecule, later identified as tRNA, interacts with amino acids rather than the triplet code passing to them directly. Marshall Nirenberg and J. Heinrich Matthaei showed in 1961 that poly-uracil RNA codes for phenylalanine. Har Gobind Khorana identified the rest of the code, and Nirenberg, Khorana and Robert W. Holley shared the 1968 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Change in the frequency of an existing allele in a population due to chance, one of the four primary forces of [[Evolution|evolution]] along with natural selection, mutation and gene flow. Drift may cause alleles to disappear, reducing genetic variation, or cause rare alleles to become frequent, possibly reaching fixation. Its effects are strongest in small populations, where fixation can occur within a few generations. In a model of 20 marbles drawn at random to form each new generation, color proportions fluctuate by chance. [[Ronald Fisher]], who explained natural selection with Mendelian genetics, held that drift played at most a minor role. In 1968 Motoo Kimura's neutral theory of molecular evolution revived the debate, claiming that most genetic changes spreading through populations result from drift acting on neutral [[Mutation|mutations]]. Founder and bottleneck effects are prominent forms, and they increase homozygosity and the risk of [[Inbreeding|inbreeding]] depression.

Manipulation of an organism's genome using technology, also called genetic modification. Recombinant [[DNA]] methods isolate, copy or synthesize DNA, which is inserted into a host organism to add genes or used to knock out existing ones. Paul Berg designed the first recombinant DNA molecule in 1972. Herbert Boyer and Stanley Cohen created the first [[Genetically modified organism|genetically modified organism]] in 1973, a bacterium. Genentech, founded in 1976, began producing human proteins, and genetically engineered human [[Insulin|insulin]] was produced in 1978. Genetically modified food has been sold since 1994, beginning with the Flavr Savr tomato. Applications include research, where [[Model organism|model organisms]] of human disease are created, medicine such as gene therapy and [[Vaccine|vaccines]], and industrial enzymes. Controversy over crops, including the destruction of early field trials by activists, led to the 2000 Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety. Regulation differs most between the [[United States]] and [[Europe]].

Organism whose genetic material has been altered using [[Genetic engineering|genetic engineering]] techniques, usually in a way that does not occur naturally by mating or recombination. Modifications can introduce new genes, enhance or knock out existing genes, and transfer genes within a species, across species or even across [[Kingdom (taxonomy)|kingdoms]]. [[Bacteria]] are the easiest organisms to engineer and are used in research, food production and drug manufacture. Plants have been engineered for research, new colors and better crops, and genetically modified crops are publicly the most controversial GMOs despite their health and environmental benefits. Most animals remain at the research stage. The first GMO was a bacterium made in 1973, and the Flavr Savr tomato, released in 1994, was the first commercialized GM food. AquAdvantage [[Salmon|salmon]] was approved for food use in 2015. Regulation differs most between the United States and Europe.

City in [[Switzerland]] (pop., 2021: 203,856), capital of the Republic and Canton of Geneva. Located where the Rhône leaves Lake Geneva, it is a global city and an international financial centre, ranked 15th by the Global Financial Centres Index in 2025. It hosts more international organizations than any other city, including agencies of the [[United Nations]], the International Committee of the Red Cross and the [[World Health Organization]]. The [[Geneva Conventions]] were signed there, and after World War I it hosted the [[League of Nations]], earning the nickname "Peace Capital". The [[Roman Republic]] took the Allobrogian border town in 121 BC. In 1541 the Protestant reformer [[John Calvin]] became its spiritual leader and established a "Protestant Rome". The Geneva metropolitan area, which extends into France, had 1,053,436 residents in 2021.

Series of four international treaties of 1949, with three additional protocols, forming the core of international humanitarian law. They set legal standards for the humane treatment of non-combatants in war, protecting civilians as well as former combatants such as prisoners of war and fighters rendered *hors de combat* by injury, illness, shipwreck or surrender. The four conventions cover the wounded and sick in the field, wounded and shipwrecked soldiers at sea, prisoners of war and civilians. Two protocols adopted in 1977 extended the rules to international and non-international armed conflicts. Their precursor of 1864 followed [[Henry Dunant]]'s observations of suffering. Aside from the UN Charter, they are among the most widely ratified international agreements, with 196 countries ratifying them in whole or with reservations. Much of their content is [[Customary law|customary law]], binding even states that are not parties.

American feral child, the pseudonym of a girl subjected to severe abuse and social isolation. From about 20 months she was kept in a locked room, strapped to a child's toilet or bound in a crib, with almost no speech or stimulation. Discovered at age 13 in 1970, she was studied intensively by linguists. She acquired a vocabulary of over 200 words and basic two- to four-word combinations but never fully acquired a first language. Her case is a key study of [[Language acquisition|language acquisition]] and the critical period hypothesis. After testing ended in 1978, institutional abuse caused physical and mental decline.

Port city (pop., 2026: 566,247) and capital of the region of Liguria, northwestern [[Italy]]. It is the busiest port in Italy and the Mediterranean Sea, and the twelfth-busiest in the [[European Union]]. The [[Republic of Genoa]] was a maritime power from the 11th century to 1797, and from the 12th to the 15th century the city led European commerce. [[Petrarch]] nicknamed it *la Superba*, meaning "the superb one". The Bank of Saint George, founded in 1407, is the oldest known state deposit bank. The historic centre, among Europe's largest and most densely populated, was listed by UNESCO in 2006. Birthplaces of notable figures include [[Christopher Columbus]] and [[Niccolò Paganini]]. Genoa forms the southern corner of the Milan–Turin–Genoa industrial triangle, with shipyards, steelworks and leading companies such as Fincantieri and Leonardo.

Attempt to deny or minimize the scale and severity of a [[Genocide|genocide]]. Denial is considered the final stage of genocide and a catalyst or indicator of future atrocities, as it includes secret planning, propaganda and destruction of evidence. Prominent examples include denial of the [[Armenian genocide]], [[Rwandan genocide]] and the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]]. Historians distinguish denial from revisionism by its techniques and motives, which often include evading moral or criminal responsibility and protecting perpetrators' reputations. Common strategies include questioning statistics, denying intent, blaming the victim, claiming self-defense and disputing the victims' group identity. Genocide scholar Adam Jones lists phrases such as "Hardly anybody died" and "It wasn't intentional". Scholars note that denial damages victims and risks future conflict, and that exposure of denial surged in the early 21st century through conspiracy theories spread on social media. Countermeasures include historical research, education and, in some jurisdictions, laws penalizing overt denial.

Socially agreed-upon style or form of communication or art, from the French word meaning kind or sort. In popular usage a genre is a category of literature, music, film or other art, defined by stylistic or thematic criteria. Works often belong to several genres by borrowing and recombining conventions. The academic study of genre is called genre studies. Critical discussion began with [[Aristotle]]'s *Poetics*, which classified poetry such as [[Ode|odes]] and epics, prose and performance, and held that comedy and [[Tragedy|tragedy]] required different speech patterns. In art history, the hierarchy of genres, strongest in France between the 17th and 19th centuries, ranked history painting above portraiture, genre painting, [[Landscape painting|landscape painting]], animal painting and still life. Genres develop over time in response to changing audiences and creators, serving as adaptable tools for making sense of art.

2020 action role-playing video game developed and published by miHoYo. Set in the fantasy world of Teyvat, with seven nations ruled by gods called Archons, it follows the Traveler, who is separated from a twin sibling after landing there. Players control a party of four characters and switch between them during real-time elemental combat. The free-to-play game is monetized through gacha mechanics and updated as a service. It was first released for [[Android (operating system)|Android]], iOS, PlayStation 4 and Windows, and reached [[PlayStation 5]] in 2021. By its fourth anniversary in 2024 it had earned US$6.3 billion in total revenue.
